title: The trivial complex character lies in the integral elementary induction ideal
statement:
Let $G$ be a finite group. A subgroup $E\leq G$ is elementary if, for some prime $p$, it is isomorphic to $C\times P$ where $C$ is a finite cyclic group with order prime to $p$ and $P$ is a finite group of order $p^a$ for some $a\geq0$. A complex representation of a finite group $J$ is a finite-dimensional complex vector space with a linear $J$-action; its character is $\chi_W(j)=\operatorname{tr}_{\mathbf C}(j\mid W)$. The coefficient field $\mathbf C$ is algebraically closed of characteristic zero [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Define $\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W$ as the quotient of $\mathbf C[G]\otimes_{\mathbf C}W$ by $[ge]\otimes w=[g]\otimes ew$, with action $a([g]\otimes w)=[ag]\otimes w$.
There are finitely many elementary subgroups $E_i\leq G$, finite-dimensional complex representations $W_i$ of $E_i$, and integers $n_i$, such that, as functions on $G$,
$$1_G=\sum_i n_i\,\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_{E_i}^G W_i}.$$
Here $1_G(g)=1$ for every $g\in G$; negative coefficients are allowed.

proof.text: Put $N=|G|\geq1$. By [lem-per-cyclotomic-integer-power-basis] choose $\zeta$, $K=\mathbf Q(\zeta)$ and its ring of integers $A$, with integral basis $1,\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{d-1}$. Let $t:A\to\mathbf Z$ take the coefficient of $1$ in this basis. Thus $t$ is $\mathbf Z$-linear and $t(1)=1$; no multiplicativity is asserted. By [lem-per-character-prime-part-reduction] every complex $G$-character takes values in $A$.

proof.text:
Let $B\subset A^G$ be the $A$-linear span of the characters of finite-dimensional complex $G$-representations. Trace of a direct sum is the sum of traces; in tensor bases the diagonal entries are products, so $\chi_{V\otimes W}=\chi_V\chi_W$. Hence $B$ is a unital subring containing the constant functions. Let $J$ be the $A$-linear span of $\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W}$ over elementary $E\leq G$ and all $E$-representations $W$. The tensor identity of [lem-per-finite-group-induction-calculus] gives
$$\chi_V\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_E^G W}=\chi_{\operatorname{Ind}_E^G(\operatorname{Res}_E^G V\otimes W)}.$$
Distributing over the finite sums defining $B,J$ shows that $J$ is an ideal of $B$. All these representations are finite-dimensional. The algebraic-closure hypothesis of the induction calculus holds by [lem-weil-complex-algebraically-closed], and $\mathbf C$ has characteristic zero.

proof.text: Suppose $J\neq B$. Since $A$ is finite free over $\mathbf Z$ by Step 1 and $G$ is finite nonempty, [lem-per-finite-function-subring-residue-test] gives $g\in G$ and a maximal ideal $\mathfrak q$ of $A$ such that $f(g)\in\mathfrak q$ for all $f\in J$. Put $k=A/\mathfrak q$ and let $r:A\to k$ be reduction; the same node gives a prime $p=\operatorname{char}(k)$. By [lem-per-character-prime-part-reduction], write $g=su$ with commuting $s,u$, the order $m$ of $s$ prime to $p$ and the order of $u$ a power of $p$. For every character, and therefore every element $f$ of its $A$-span $B$, one has $r(f(g))=r(f(s))$. Thus $r(f(s))=0$ for every $f\in J$.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation lifting before (5), motivation only. Agent-written character-ring proof; WANTED Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, Part II Chapter 10, sections 10.2-10.3.

proof.text:
Let $D=C_G(s)$ and $C=\langle s\rangle\leq D$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-sylow-subgroup-prime-index] to the finite group $D$ and prime $p$, obtaining $P\leq D$ of $p$-power order with $p\nmid[D:P]$. The subgroup $C$ is central in $D$. Since $|C|=m$ is prime to $p$, $C\cap P=\{1\}$: the order of an element of the intersection divides both $m$ and $|P|$. Thus multiplication $(c,v)\mapsto cv$ is an injective homomorphism $C\times P\to G$. Its image $E=CP$ is elementary, $|E|=m|P|$, and
$$c_0=[D:E]=|D|/(m|P|)$$
is an integer prime to $p$, since $[D:P]=m c_0$ is prime to $p$. Cosets give the displayed order and index equalities.

proof.text:
Let $S=C\cap s^G$, so $s\in S$. As $m\mid N$, $\xi=\zeta^{N/m}$ is a primitive $m$th root. For $0\leq j<m$ define $\lambda_j(s^a v)=\xi^{ja}$ for $v\in P$; uniqueness in $C\times P$ makes this a well-defined homomorphism $E\to\mathbf C^\times$. Put $a_j=\sum_{s^a\in S}\xi^{ja}\in A$. In $A\subset\mathbf C$ the finite geometric-sum calculation gives
$$\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\xi^{-j}a_j=\sum_{s^a\in S}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\xi^{j(a-1)}=m.$$
Indeed the inner sum is $m$ when $a=1$ modulo $m$; otherwise multiplying it by the nonzero number $\xi^{a-1}-1$ gives $\xi^{m(a-1)}-1=0$, so it vanishes in $\mathbf C$. This also covers $m=1$. As $r(m)\neq0$, at least one $r(a_j)$ is nonzero.

source.place: Expose X Proposition 1.2, printed p.138, representation lifting before (5), motivation only. Agent-written character-ring proof; WANTED Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups, Part II Chapter 10, sections 10.2-10.3.

proof.text:
Write $U_i=\operatorname{Ind}_{E_i}^G W_i$. By [lem-per-finite-group-character-decomposition], decompose the finitely many $U_i$ into irreducibles and group isomorphic summands; also include the trivial line $T_0$. The field hypothesis is supplied by [lem-weil-complex-algebraically-closed]. For the resulting finite list of pairwise nonisomorphic $T$, let $m_{iT}\in\mathbf Z_{\geq0}$ be the multiplicity in $U_i$. Pair the character equality of Step 6 with $\chi_T(g^{-1})$ and divide by $|G|$. The orthogonality statement [lem-per-finite-group-character-orthogonality] gives
$$\sum_i b_i m_{iT}=\delta_{T,T_0}$$
in $\mathbf C$ and hence in its subring $A$. Apply the $\mathbf Z$-linear coefficient map $t$ of Step 1 to get $\sum_i t(b_i)m_{iT}=\delta_{T,T_0}$. Multiplying these integer equalities by $\chi_T$ and summing over the finite list yields
$$1_G=\sum_i t(b_i)\chi_{U_i}.$$
Set $n_i=t(b_i)\in\mathbf Z$. The elementary subgroups and quotient induction are exactly those of the statement. The coefficient map was applied only to equalities of multiplicities, not to character values multiplied by arbitrary elements of $A$.
